ox: Correct. With the object beyond 2f, the lens bends light to a real image between f and 2f on the far side. It is upside down (inverted) and smaller than the object.
Wrong. A virtual, upright, larger image is the magnifying-glass case, which needs the object inside f. The trap is mixing up the object zones.
Wrong. Real, inverted, larger happens when the object is between f and 2f. Students swap the two zones.
Wrong. No image forms (rays come out parallel) when the object sits exactly at f, not beyond 2f.

p: A converging lens bends light rays toward a point. f is the focal length, the distance where parallel rays meet. 2f is twice that distance. A real image is one that light actually reaches, so it can be shown on a screen.
Far objects (beyond 2f) make small, upside-down, real images. As the object moves closer, the image grows.

q57.eli: Think of a camera photographing a faraway tree. The picture on the sensor is tiny and upside down.
mem: Beyond 2f: real, inverted, smaller, image between f and 2f
At 2f: real, inverted, same size, image at 2f
Between f and 2f: real, inverted, larger
Inside f: virtual, upright, larger

tb.cap: Object position for a converging lens

q57.trap: Mixing up which zone gives a smaller image and which gives a larger one. Far object means small image.

ox: Correct. The moving ambulance squeezes the sound waves in front of it. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency, so you hear a higher pitch (Doppler effect).
Wrong. Lower pitch is heard when the source moves away. The trap is reversing the direction.
Wrong. Loudness (amplitude) may change, but the question asks about pitch, and pitch (frequency) does change. The option wrongly says it stays the same.
Wrong. The pitch is higher, but the reason is false. Sound speed is set by the medium (air), not by the moving source.

p: Frequency is how many waves reach your ear each second. Your brain hears frequency as pitch. When a source moves toward you, each new wave starts closer to you, so the waves bunch up.
Bunched waves have a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency. The wave speed stays the same because it depends only on the medium.

q58.eli: Imagine a friend tossing balls to you while running toward you. The balls arrive more often than if he stood still.
mem: Toward you: higher frequency, higher pitch
Away from you: lower frequency, lower pitch
Wave speed depends on the medium, not the source
q58.trap: Saying sound speeds up. The speed does not change; the wavelength shrinks.

ox: Correct. Photon energy is E = hf. Ultraviolet has the highest frequency of these choices, so it has the most energy.
Wrong. Red visible light has a lower frequency than UV, so less energy. Red is the lowest-energy visible color.
Wrong. Infrared sits below visible light in frequency, so its photons carry less energy.
Wrong. Microwaves have the lowest frequency here, so the least energy. The trap is picking the one that sounds most powerful, like microwave ovens.

p: Light comes in packets called photons. Each photon's energy equals Planck's constant (h) times its frequency (f). Higher frequency means more energy.
From low to high energy: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

q59.eli: Think of shaking a rope. Faster shaking (higher frequency) puts more energy into each wiggle.
mem: E = hf = hc/wavelength
High frequency means short wavelength and high energy
Order: radio, micro, IR, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma

fm.f: E = hf, where E = photon energy, h = Planck's constant, f = frequency
fm.v: h is the same for all photons; UV has the largest f of the choices
fm.s: Largest f gives largest E, so UV
fm.why: Energy is directly proportional to frequency.
fm.nc: No numbers needed; just compare frequencies.

q59.mn: Roy G. Biv orders visible light: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet. Red has the least energy and violet the most.
q59.trap: Confusing wavelength with energy. Longer wavelength means lower energy.

ox: Wrong. Decibels use a logarithm, so a 100-fold intensity change is not +100 dB. The trap is treating the scale as linear.
Correct. The change in level is 10 x log(100) = 10 x 2 = 20 dB.
Wrong. The log of 100 is 2, but you must multiply by 10. This answer forgets the factor of 10.
Wrong. Decibel changes add or subtract. They are not multiplied, since the scale is logarithmic.

p: The decibel (dB) scale measures sound level using a logarithm. A logarithm asks: 10 to what power gives this number? So log of 100 is 2.
Because of this, multiplying intensity by a factor adds a fixed number of dB. Each factor of 10 adds 10 dB.

q60.eli: Like a video game where each level needs ten times more points. The level number goes up by 1 while the points jump tenfold.
mem: Factor of 10 in intensity = +10 dB
Factor of 100 = +20 dB; factor of 1000 = +30 dB
dB changes add; intensities multiply

fm.f: change in dB = 10 x log(I2/I1), where I1 = starting intensity, I2 = new intensity, log = power of 10
fm.why: Sound level is defined on a logarithmic scale.
fm.nc: Count the zeros in 100 (two), then multiply by 10.

ox: Correct. A strong, sharp peak near 1710 cm-1 is the signature of a C=O (carbonyl) stretch in a ketone, aldehyde, or similar group.
Wrong. An alcohol O-H gives a broad peak around 3200-3550 cm-1, and the question says that peak is absent.
Wrong. A nitrile C triple bond N stretch appears near 2250 cm-1, not 1710.
Wrong. An alkyne C-H gives a sharp peak near 3300 cm-1, far from 1710. Students match any 'sharp' peak without checking the position.

p: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy shows which bonds are in a molecule. Each bond vibrates at a set wavenumber (cm-1). A peak at that position tells you the bond is there.
The key peaks: C=O near 1700 (strong, sharp), O-H near 3300 (broad), C triple bond N near 2250.

mem: C=O: ~1700 cm-1, strong and sharp
O-H alcohol: ~3300 cm-1, broad; carboxylic acid O-H is even broader
C triple bond N: ~2250; C triple bond C: ~2100-2250
N-H: ~3300, sharper than O-H
q61.trap: Choosing by shape alone. Check both position and shape.

ox: Wrong. Air is a gas with widely spaced particles, so sound is slowest here (about 340 m/s).
Wrong. Water is faster than air (about 1500 m/s) but slower than steel. The trap is stopping at the first faster medium.
Correct. Steel is a stiff solid (about 5000 m/s). Sound speed rises with stiffness of the medium, so solids are fastest.
Wrong. Sound is a mechanical wave and needs particles to travel. In a vacuum it does not travel at all.

p: Sound is a mechanical wave. It moves by particles bumping into neighbors. Stiffer materials pass the bump along faster.
So sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases. In a vacuum there are no particles, so no sound.

q62.eli: Think of a row of dominoes. If they are tightly connected and stiff, the push moves quickly.
mem: Solid > liquid > gas for sound speed
Sound cannot travel in a vacuum
Light is different: it does travel through a vacuum
q62.trap: Thinking denser always means faster. Stiffness matters most.
